12975-international-weekly-miscellany-of:
The International Weekly Miscellany, volume one, number two, dated July 8, 1850, is a New York journal of literature, art, and science. It praises The Lorgnette as the cleverest book of its kind since Irving and Paulding's Salmagundi, soon to appear in two volumes with drawings by Darley. The author promises harmless ridicule of the day's follies without naming persons.

A tale inside mixes love and science, as a lover tells Marguerite that a fading star named Dumiger proves his sums, then shows her a fine clock behind a curtain. The issue shows mid-century American readers sampling foreign letters, satire, and popular science in one weekly bundle.
12982-international-weekly-miscellany-of:
The International Weekly Miscellany, volume one, number three, dated July 15, 1850, opens with George Sand and her promised Memoirs of my Life. The journal reports she was paid between thirty and forty thousand dollars, and that the Paris Credit bought the right to print the first six volumes in its feuilleton for twelve thousand. Readers expect both generous character and reckless confession.

A California piece follows, as a traveler visits the diggings and finds Fremont and King confirmed on gold, health, and hard work. The issue thus mixes French literary gossip with gold-rush news for New York readers.
13053-international-weekly-miscellany-of:
The International Weekly Miscellany, volume one, number four, dated July 22, 1850, opens with Paris literary coteries of the last century. It notes how salons run by Mesdames de Tencin, Pompadour, Geoffrin, Deffant, and L'Espinasse are being revived under the new Republic, with American echoes in Boston, Philadelphia, and Charleston.

A domestic tale inside turns on a father begging his son for a few shillings, after giving up his whole business to the boy, who now keeps him on an allowance. The issue pairs French salon history with American fiction and letters for its weekly readers.
13241-international-weekly-miscellany-of:
The International Weekly Miscellany, volume one, number five, New York, July 29, 1850, mixes literature, art, and science for a general audience. Its opening piece, Tea-Smuggling in Russia, notes that smuggling histories abound in curiosities few ever hear, since smugglers keep their tales close. Frontier lore, it says, lives in old men's memories.

No frontier is richer, the piece claims, than Spain and France, where Pyrenean recesses shelter half-robbers driving contraband. Later pages give verse on shadows, false peace, and wasted arms letting slip flowers, and a tale of Irish letters, armorial wax, and an aunt's rent charge. The number is a mid-century miscellany, worldly and varied.
13643-international-weekly-miscellany-of:
Volume one, number six, of the International Weekly Miscellany, dated August 5, 1850, offers literature, art, and science from both sides of the Atlantic. It opens with German criticism of English women novelists, ranking Miss Jewsbury, Miss Bronte, and Mrs. Gaskell in the first rank for novels drawn from country and middle-class life.

Later pages turn to American politics, with bitter verses on Northern truckling to the South and a pro-slavery speech by Calhoun set to music, alongside fiction and foreign news. The mix shows a New York weekly trying to keep American readers in touch with European letters. It is a lively snapshot of literary journalism just before the Civil War.
13711-international-weekly-miscellany-of:
The International Weekly Miscellany for August 12, 1850, gathers foreign news for American readers. Its lead piece, translated from a Paris letter, discusses women and literature in France. It notes that French women, despite talk of emancipation, already held strong social power in Paris. Other items cover books, art, and science abroad.

Short notices track writers, ministers, and new publications in Europe and America. The miscellany aimed to keep New York readers in touch with London and Paris. Its tone is brisk and gossipy, with room for serious comment. The issue captures mid-century transatlantic culture. It also shows how American editors borrowed freely from foreign papers.
13796-international-weekly-miscellany-of:
The International Weekly Miscellany for August 19, 1850, leads with theatre in Russia and Poland. Translated from the Leipzig Grenzboten, the sketch describes drama under the czar. It argues that a people's theatre reveals its literary strength and public life. Russian stages, still young, lagged behind poetry and prose.

Other items in the issue cover foreign books, art, and science. The editors aimed to give American readers fresh European news each week. Short, translated pieces dominate, with brief editorial comment. The Russia article also hints at censorship and social control. As a periodical sample, it shows mid-century American interest in the wider world.
13797-international-weekly-miscellany-of:
Dated August 26, 1850, this number of the International Weekly Miscellany leads with numismatic archaeology. A magnificent Paris work, begun fifteen years earlier under Delaroche and Lenormand, had just been completed. It ranges from regal coins of Syracuse and the Ptolemies to modern issues. The editors praise its scope and learning.

Other pieces cover horse-chasing on the heath, without saddle or stirrup, and foreign literary news. Short items keep American readers abreast of European books and art. The miscellany's brisk, borrowed style suits a weekly digest. This issue shows mid-century fascination with coins as art and history. It also captures the pace of transatlantic journalism.
18222-the-religion-of-numa-and-other-ess:
Jesse Benedict Carter wrote The Religion of Numa and Other Essays on the Religion of Ancient Rome, printed in London and New York by Macmillan in 1906. Carter, a scholar of Roman religion, dedicates the book to K. F. C.

Essays run from the religion of Numa and the reorganization of Servius to the coming of the Sibyl, the decline of faith, and the Augustan renaissance. Carter argues that Rome, like nations, grew by contact with the outside world, through Punic wars and Greek lore. The book is a clear, classic study of Roman faith, still useful for students of ancient religion.
18557-the-battle-of-principles-a-study-o:
Newell Dwight Hillis wrote this study of the anti-slavery conflict, treating its heroes and its eloquence as a battle of principles. Twelve chapters move from the rise of American slavery and the growth of the traffic to the battle lines drawn by Webster and Calhoun.

Later chapters take up Garrison and Phillips in agitation, Sumner and the educated men, Greeley and the common people, Stowe and John Brown, and Lincoln and Douglas in debate. The book closes with secession, Beecher's appeal to England, soldiers and sailors, the people at home, and Lincoln as martyred president.
21200-the-letters-of-cicero-volume-1-the:
Evelyn S. Shuckburgh translated the whole surviving correspondence of Cicero into English, arranged in time order, for this four-volume edition published in London in 1899. Volume One covers the years 68 to 52 BC. Shuckburgh had also translated Polybius and written a history of Rome.

Cicero's letters, kept by his freedman Tiro, begin only in Cicero's thirty-ninth year, so no boyhood letters survive. What remains deals closely with daily politics: elections, trials, exile, and family matters. The letters let readers watch the late Roman Republic through the eyes of its greatest speaker, writing frankly to friends like Atticus about each crisis.
22778-the-remarkable-adventures-of-an-ol:
The Remarkable Adventures of an Old Woman and Her Pig is an ancient nursery tale in verse. Its cumulative story follows a dame whose pig will not jump over the stile. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. Every child once knew the chain: the dog must bite the pig, the stick must beat the dog, and so on down the line.

The dame, out of patience, cries in a fright to a passing dog. Pray, give Piggy a bite, she begs, and compel him over the stile. Or here I may stay till midnight. Mr. Bow-wow, of course, hears the request, but silently stands without saying a word. Her threats of being even with him only lengthen the chain. Such tales taught rhythm, memory, and comic exasperation to the youngest readers.
26182-the-rover-boys-on-the-plains-or-th:
Arthur M. Winfield's 1906 volume, the tenth Rover Boys book, sends Dick, Tom, and Sam from a houseboat on the Mississippi onto the great plains. Chapters promise a big lumber raft, a pepper ghost, a storm, a runaway steer, and a cowboy named Jim Jones. The boys meet old foe Dan Baxter again, and they help unravel the mystery around a lonely ranch.

Bank bills on a table, a night scare, a snakes' den, and the burning of the ranch all drive the plot toward a round-up finish. Written for young readers, the book mixes river travel, prairie adventure, and schoolboy pluck. It stands alone as a tale, though it rewards readers who have followed the brothers from school onward.
2655-the-papers-and-writings-of-abraham-:
Abraham Lincoln's third volume in the Constitutional Edition holds the first part of the Lincoln Douglas debates, edited by Arthur Brooks Lapsley. The senatorial campaign of 1858 in Illinois set Lincoln against Stephen A. Douglas in a contest over slavery's future.

The volume opens at Springfield on June 17, 1858, with the House Divided speech, and follows the campaign's early clashes. Lincoln's logic, Douglas's fire, and the crowds that heard them come alive in full text. The book is essential for understanding how a prairie lawyer became a national voice. The debates drew crowds across Illinois, and newspapers carried them nationwide.
2656-the-papers-and-writings-of-abraham-:
Abraham Lincoln's fourth volume in the Constitutional Edition holds the second part of the Lincoln Douglas debates, edited by Arthur Brooks Lapsley. The volume opens with the fourth debate, at Charleston on September 18, 1858, where Lincoln warns how hard it will be to be heard fairly.

Douglas and Lincoln spar over slavery, popular sovereignty, and the Dred Scott decision, before crowds that hung on every word. The full texts let readers judge the arguments as Illinois heard them. The book completes the debate record, and shows Lincoln sharpening the case that carried him to the White House.
27253-the-discovery-of-america-vol-1-of-:
John Fiske's The Discovery of America, volume one of two, covers ancient America and the Spanish conquest. It was copyrighted in 1892 and published by Houghton, Mifflin in 1897. An Emerson epigraph opens the book: paths lead out, the exodus of nations, men dispersed to all shores.

The volume moves from wolf, turtle, and turkey phratries to Norse voyages. Thorfinn Karlsefni comes to Brattahlid in the summer of 1006, falls in love with the widow Gudrid, and marries her that winter. Fiske writes a broad, readable history of America before and after Columbus.
30285-how-i-filmed-the-war-a-record-of-t:
Lieutenant Geoffrey H. Malins, holder of the Order of the British Empire, records how he filmed the Great War, in a Herbert Jenkins volume from London in 1920. Low Warren, then editor of the Kinematograph Weekly, arranged the manuscript Malins sent from France, and Malins states it stands unaltered in any material respect. A front picture shows him filming the preliminary bombardment of the Big Push on July 1, 1916.

Minutes after that photograph, a shell burst within six yards, smashing trench walls and half burying the cameraman, who had hung a sandbag on wire before his lens for camouflage. Part 1 opens with a few words of introduction, then follows Malins with the Belgians at Ramscapelle, reaching first-line trenches and serving as a Belgian soldier for a time. The book gives the Somme battles through a camera lens.
30478-vegetable-diet-as-sanctioned-by-me:
Dr. William A. Alcott argues for a vegetable diet in a second edition, revised and enlarged, published in New York in 1859 and first entered for copyright in 1849. He asks whether any animal food is absolutely necessary for the full development of human nature, and notes that no practical, moderate volume on the subject yet existed in Europe or America.

Alcott cites medical men and experience in all ages, then adds a system of vegetable cookery so readers can put theory into practice. As author of guides for young men, young women, mothers, and housekeepers, he writes for households. The book blends health advice, moral argument, and recipes into an early American case for eating plants.
3273-the-complete-works-of-artemus-ward-:
Part three of Artemus Ward's complete works holds his stories and romances. Moses the Sassy, or the disguised duke, leads the set, opening in the classic precincts of Boston. Marion, a romance of the French school, and William Barker, the young patriot, follow. A romance of the conscript and one of only a mechanic keep the patriotic humor running.

Roberto the rover, a tale of sea and shore, and Red Hand, a tale of revenge, widen the range. Pyrotechny, a romance after the French, and the last of the Culkinses follow, with a Mormon romance, Reginald Gloverson, to close. Ward tells each tale in his famous misspelling, where high romance meets low comedy and both come out laughing.
32823-narrative-of-a-journey-to-the-summ:
William Howard, M.D., tells of his climb to the summit of Mont Blanc in July 1819, published at Baltimore by Fielding Lucas Jr. in 1821. Howard wrote the account a few days after the climb, while confined to his chamber, and it first appeared in the Analectic Magazine for May 1820.

Howard had already climbed Vesuvius and Aetna within a few months, and he calls Mont Blanc the highest point in Europe, save the Himalaya mountains in India. His party reached the Grand Mulet at eleven thousand feet, eight thousand above Chamouny, after walking fourteen or fifteen miles for four or five in a straight line. A snow bridge sank beneath them on the descent, and they spent a night imprisoned on the rock.
33122-an-impromptu-ascent-of-mont-blanc:
W. H. Le Mesurier's Impromptu Ascent of Mont Blanc tells how a mountain climb came about on the spur of the moment and what it cost in effort and awe. It was published in London in 1882. Illustrations show Chamonix, the summit, and the glaciers, while later plates follow the route and the descent.

Le Mesurier opens with a question to fresh breaking day and the mountains: why are ye beautiful? The narrative answers by walking, climbing, and looking, with a diagram comparing the heights of Mont Blanc and Snowdon and a map of routes to Chamonix. It is a short, vivid mountaineering memoir from the age when Alpine climbing was still an adventure for determined amateurs, and it keeps its sense of wonder intact.
3721-france-and-england-in-north-america:
Francis Parkman opens his great history of France and England in North America with the first French ventures in the New World. Norman, Breton, and Basque fishermen worked the cod banks of Newfoundland before most maps showed the coast, and their seasonal voyages led the way for explorers, traders, and priests. Parkman sets these small beginnings against large forces, as feudal lords, kings, and the church sought to plant their order on a new continent.

The volume argues that tiny strifes on a far shore shaped the fate of peoples, since the contest between French rule and English freedom began in these camps and coves. Parkman writes with color and care, and his scenes of sea, forest, and native towns still draw readers. Later volumes carry the story to war and conquest, but this first book shows where the French claim began.
4635-tom-swift-and-his-great-searchlight:
Victor Appleton sends Tom Swift to the border for Uncle Sam in this boys' adventure, built around a searchlight. The contents move from a scrap of paper and a spy in town, through queer repairs and searching for smugglers. Then come a raid, an appeal to Tom, and the plain need for a searchlight. Tom's newest invention answers that need, with a warning to beware of the comet, and a trip off for the border.

Andy Foger's new airship, a false clue, and a rescue on the lake follow. Then come Koku's prisoner, what an Indian saw, a pursuit, dire peril, and Ned missing, before a night race and a capture close the book. Koku saves the light at a key hour, and Tom's machine turns darkness into an ally. Readers get a fast, patriotic inventors' tale, full of smugglers, airships, and loyal friends, in the classic Tom Swift manner.
9917-your-child-today-and-tomorrow-some-:
Sidonie Matzner Gruenberg's book for parents takes up the everyday problems of raising children: punishment, reasoning, lies, ideals, ambitions, fear, work, play, imagination, and obedience. She treats each topic as a question parents actually face, not as abstract theory.

Chapters discuss the lies children tell, being afraid, the training of the will, children's gangs and friendships, and the passage into adolescence, with heredity and the golden age of transition. Gruenberg writes in a calm, practical voice. Parents get a humane, early twentieth-century guide that still speaks to common worries today.
britannica-1911-franc:
The franc is a French coin, current at different periods and of varying values. The first coin of the name was struck in gold by John II of France in 1360. It bore the legend Johannes Dei gracia Francorum rex, John by the grace of God king of the Franks, and from that legend, it is said, the name came. It also bore King John on horseback, so it was called a franc a cheval.

On Charles's coin the king stood upright under a Gothic canopy, and it was termed a franc a pied, a franc on foot. As a coin the franc vanished after Charles VI, but the name lived on as another word for the livre tournois of twenty sols. In 1795 the livre was replaced, and the entry follows the franc into its modern life as France's standard coin.
britannica-1911-lanfranc:
Lanfranc appears in this 1911 account from his years as a famed teacher at Bec, where pupils came from France, Normandy, Gascony, Flanders, Germany, and Italy. Logic and church teaching were his chief subjects. One pupil, Anselm of Badagio, later became Pope Alexander II, and Bec stood at the heart of a wider reform movement.

Against Berengar of Tours he defended the church view of the sacrament at councils in 1050, 1054, and 1059, and his later tract on the subject became a school text. Reconciled with Duke William, he won papal approval for William's marriage, became abbot at Caen in 1066, and took the English primacy in 1070 after Stigand fell. He rebuilt church order in England and died on 24 May 1089.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-anthony-blanc:
Anthony Blanc, fifth Bishop and first Archbishop of New Orleans, born 1792, died 1860. He was among the first students after the Church's restoration in France, ordained in 1816 by Dubourg at Lyons, seeking American mission volunteers. He came to America in September 1817, landing at Annapolis. He then went with Dubourg to New Orleans and for fifteen years led an arduous missionary life.

Appeals to the Legislature dragged a controversy out for over a year, but he won every issue. In 1838 he established a diocesan seminary and introduced the Lazarists, Jesuits, Redemptorists, and Christian Brothers. He attended the first Baltimore Plenary Council and was in Rome for the Immaculate Conception proclamation in 1854. New Orleans became an archbishopric in 1850; he received the pallium in 1851. During his tenure abuses were corrected; churches grew from 26 to 73, priests from 27 to 92, and schools testified to his zeal. He died suddenly at home, active to the last.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lanfranc:
Lanfranc (about 1005-1089) was Archbishop of Canterbury, born at Pavia. Liberally educated despite early orphanhood, he became a successful lawyer before leaving Italy to pursue learning in France. At Avranches in Normandy he won fame as a teacher.

Drawn to religious life, he slipped away to Bec and joined Abbot Herluin's poor new community. As prior he opened a school that drew scholars from across Europe, among them the future Pope Alexander II and Anselm, his successor at Bec and Canterbury. At Rome in May 1050 he opposed Berengar's teaching on the Eucharist. His masterly defence fixed him ever since as the chief exponent of Transubstantiation, a doctrine he expounded rather than invented.
doe-osti-2584398-benchmark-tracking-syst:
PNNL report 38155, by Braedon Billingsley and Joseph Cottam in August 2025, builds a memory for software benchmarks. The subject is Lamellar, an asynchronous runtime for high-performance computing developed at Pacific Northwest National Laboratory. Before this work, Lamellar's benchmark results were hard to track across code versions, so slow regressions could hide inside routine commits. The project set out to make performance history systematic and searchable.

Three pieces compose the system. Benchmark output was standardized into JSON Line records carrying execution time, hardware, and environment fields. Results are versioned in a dedicated git repository, chosen after weighing other data stores. A suite of Python tools enriches results with metadata and supports queries across commit history, hardware configurations, and benchmark variants. A cheap first-pass check trims the computing cost of comparisons. For a runtime whose whole purpose is speed, knowing exactly when it got slower is the point.
doe-osti-3024393-development-of-local-hy: Density functionals got hybrid-developed, and this DOE text treats self-interaction errors. The pages detail the local findings. The chemists get their data. The effects were many-electron. The data were chemist. The error was self-interaction. The functionals were density.
doe-osti-3028351-annual-summary-report-f: 200 West got FY2025-assessed, and this DOE annual covers low-level waste. The pages detail the performance findings. The nuclear folks get their data. The disposal was waste. The data were nuclear. The 200 were West. The low-level were waste.
doe-osti-3028370-annual-summary-report-f: The Integrated Disposal Facility getting its yearly checkup got the DOE FY2025 review, and this annual grades the waste burial. The pages detail the results. The nuclear folks get their data. The review was performance. The burial were waste. The checkup were yearly.
doe-osti-3028383-annual-summary-report-f: The Environmental Restoration Disposal Facility getting its yearly checkup got the DOE FY2025 review, and this annual grades the cleanup burial. The pages detail the results. The nuclear folks get their data. The review was performance. The burial were cleanup.
doe-osti-3028394-annual-summary-report-f: 200 East got FY2025-assessed, and this DOE annual covers low-level waste. The pages detail the performance findings. The nuclear folks get their data. The disposal was waste. The data were nuclear. The 200 were East. The assessment were performance. The East were 200.
doe-osti-3384905-evaluating-lithium-lead: Li-Pb got tritium-bred, and this DOE text evaluates blanket mixtures. The pages detail the increased findings. The nuclear folks get their data. The systems were fusion energy. The data were nuclear. The blanket were exploring. The tritium were breeding.
doe-osti-3674462-ciepat-for-photovoltaic: CIEPAT got resilience-slid, and this DOE slides cover photovoltaic system resilience. The pages detail the CIEPAT findings. The energy folks get their deck. The format was slides. The deck was energy. The CIEPAT were system. The resilience were photovoltaic.
doe-osti-3874818-final-scientific-techni: Heat pipe reactors got AM-finalled, and this DOE final covers embedded nuclear hybrid. The pages detail the scientific findings. The nuclear folks get their closeout. The report was technical. The closeout was nuclear. The embedded were heat pipe. The hybrid were nuclear.
france-and-england-in-north-america-part:
Francis Parkman, the American historian of the French era, opened his France and England in North America series with Pioneers of France in the New World. Parkman framed the struggle as a contest of systems. Feudalism, monarchy, and Rome, he argues, tried to master a continent through New France. Protestant New England grew the opposite way, from fugitive settlers and freedom.

French soldiers, priests, and traders push into forests, map rivers, and raise forts. Huguenot settlers in Florida, Champlain's work in Canada, and the missions of Jesuit priests carry the thread. Parkman stresses that New France stayed all head: king, noble, and priest directed, while the settler body stayed thin. English colonies, poorer in glory, grew muscle, numbers, and staying power. His prose rolls with scenery, battles, and sketches of explorers. Readers starting Parkman's epic begin here, where the French adventure shines brightest and its weakness shows.
govdocs-archive_org-TerrestrialPlaneTheF: Material on Frederick Henry Cook, the polar explorer whose claim to have reached the North Pole was famously disputed, makes up this file, under the heading Terrestrial Plane. The capture is incomplete and garbled, so large parts of the original work cannot be read as scanned. It is preserved as found, a partial record kept for whatever its surviving pages still offer researchers of the polar exploration controversies.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-DunBradstreetIn: In January 1976, Dun & Bradstreet issued a business information report on Harold Weisberg, listed in the file as HD Weisberg ONR. Dun & Bradstreet reports rate the standing of a business for lenders and suppliers. The surviving record gives the report's date and subject but not its ratings or contents, so it stands as a credit agency's file entry on the Kennedy assassination researcher.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-PressResearchIn:
A newspaper article reports on Press Research Inc., a service that sold interpretive reports to subscriber newspapers. One report caused a fight: a 45,000-word study of Thomas Dewey, the Republican candidate, which Democrats bought. The article also covers reports that booklets attacking Dewey were being burned.

Interpretive-report services sold analysis to editors who wanted background with a slant measured to order. A 45,000-word report bought by one party, and booklets burned by someone, made the service itself the story. The article preserves the episode's elements: the company, the report's size, the buyers, and the burnings. It is a look at the information trade inside a presidential campaign of the 1940s.
international-weekly-miscellany-of-liter:
Various writers filled the International Weekly Miscellany for July 8, 1850, at New York. It was volume one, number two. The issue praises The Lorgnette, a book of town studies, as the cleverest of its kind since Irving. Its author's plan is quoted, to ridicule foibles without personal attack.

Fiction inside sets a nervous father in a colonnade of choice flowers. Frederick is greeted by a tall, gray-bearded man in stately black with a golden chain. Court scenes, poems, and reprinted essays fill the pages. The weekly aimed to give American readers a mixed literary feast.
nasa-tm-19670030533-certain-general-patt:
B. A. Kolachev, V. A. Livanov, N. Ya. Gusel'nikov, and A. A. Bukhanova wrote this study in Russian, published in 1965. It seeks general patterns in hydrogen brittleness in two titanium alloys, VT3-1 and VT15. Hydrogen can sneak into titanium and make it crack like glass. The translation was issued at Redstone Arsenal in July 1967.

Brittleness in VT3-1, they show, develops most strongly below room temperature and at low strain rates. Beta alloys like VT15 are also prone below room temperature, in a narrow range and only when strained slowly. The authors trace the cause to processes in the beta phase during deformation. Both alloys, they conclude, turn brittle in much the same manner.
nasa-tm-19700025196-preliminary-lunar-or:
E. C. Howell, C. R. Hunt, and V. W. Simmons of the TRW Systems Group wrote this internal note for the Manned Spacecraft Center. It is dated February 21, 1969. It gives a first lunar orbit attitude sequence for Mission F, the Apollo 10 flight, which rehearsed the landing without touching down.

The sequence walks revolution by revolution through the spacecraft's time in lunar orbit. Steps cover the crew's sleep period, then undocking and the descent orbit insertion burn. Later steps run from that burn's cutoff through the phasing, insertion, and circularization burns. Each step is paired with figures, so planners could see the planned pointing at every stage.
nasa-tm-19700025414-evaluation-of-manned:
Tommie L. Wheeler and Edgar A. Dalie of the Manned Spacecraft Center in Houston wrote this evaluation of prelaunch checkout. For three or four years, center staff had been bringing the ACE-S/C checkout system into Apollo work. That system ran the tests of the command, service, and lunar modules before launch.

Day-to-day use taught the staff where the system fell short. They fixed running problems and drew up design changes as they went. The paper judges how well the system meets the true test needs of the spacecraft. Checkout quality decides whether faults are caught on the ground, where they can still be fixed.
nasa-tm-19710002734-overall-performance-:
Carl Weigel Jr., Edward R. Tysl, and Calvin L. Ball of the Lewis Research Center wrote this report in November 1970. It gives the overall performance of a small centrifugal compressor running on argon gas. The wheel carries sweptback blades and serves gas loop power systems.

Performance is charted against the weight of gas flowing through the machine. At the design flow and tip speed, the compressor reached the pressure rise and efficiency the abstract records. The best efficiency at design speed came at a somewhat lower flow. Compressors of this size drive the working gas around closed Brayton power loops for space.
nasa-tm-19710023020-atlas-centaur-ac-19-:
Lewis Research Center staff reviewed two Atlas Centaur launches in this July 1971 memorandum, NASA TM X-2278. Vehicles AC-19 and AC-20 carried the Mariner Mars probes of 1969. Both used a direct, single burn ascent. AC-20 placed Mariner VI on its path, and AC-19 placed Mariner VII. The launches took place in the first quarter of 1969.

Mariner VI flew past Mars on an equatorial pass on July 31, 1969. Five days later, Mariner VII passed over the planet's south pole. The report discusses how each launch vehicle performed in flight. Such postflight reviews confirmed the Atlas Centaur as a reliable planetary launcher. They also fed lessons into later missions.
nasa-tm-19720004682-ionospheric-nf-sub-h:
A NASA preprint numbered X-621-71-214 studies echoes that the Alouette 2 satellite picked up in the upper air. The scan leaves its author names unreadable. The echoes sat near harmonics of the electron gyro rate, the rate at which electrons circle in Earth's field. Their frequencies sat slightly off the values that field models predicted.

Plasma wave effects, the paper reports, can explain the shifts in a consistent way. Two offsets also play a part. One is a small positive offset in the sounder transmitter's own frequency. The other is a small negative offset in Earth's field, set against the model field. Large positive shifts once blamed on the echoes themselves can instead come from the instrument offset. The field offset fits with magnetic readings taken by the OGO 3 and OGO 5 satellites at higher altitudes.
podcast-dannyjones-R3I2yU1mfNc:
Historian Rebecca Lemov wrote a history of brainwashing research and now studies the sciences of mind control at Harvard. On Danny Jones's podcast, she explains why she fears MK-Ultra, the CIA's notorious mind control program, is still active in modern forms, carried on by new institutions with better tools.

Lemov's authority is archival; she has read the program's surviving records and interviewed its world. She connects the Cold War experiments to today's data-driven influence systems with a scholar's care for the differences. Jones draws out the continuities that alarm her. The episode offers the strongest historically grounded version of a popular fear, from the person best qualified to judge the original. Listeners can weigh her evidence for survival of the program's spirit against the official story of its burial.
podcast-dannyjones-XyVKTJYxmnc:
George Howard joins Danny Jones to talk about the search for Sodom and Gomorrah, the two cities destroyed in the Bible. The episode title says scholars of the Bible have found the lost city. Howard speaks for the dig and its claims.

Howard lays out the site, the layer of ash and ruin, and why his team links it to the Bible story. He also deals with the doubts raised by other scholars who place the cities elsewhere. Jones walks through the finds one by one. Listeners get a field report from a dig that claims to match one of the most famous tales in scripture.
podcast-dannyjones-vZZqv0SYAnc:
Historian John Newman returns to Danny Jones with newly freed JFK files he says prove a Russian mole sat inside the CIA. Newman has read the case files for decades. The mole claim goes to the heart of Cold War spy lore.

Newman walks through the new pages and the names they clear or cloud. He argues the mole hunt tore the agency in half and still shapes how it acts. Jones asks what the files at last settle. Listeners who love spy craft get a dense, rich talk. The library holds it as an archive record of his reading.
podcast-tuckercarlson-DE2AVar-XNc:
Maine reporter Steve Robinson joins Tucker Carlson to expose a drug network in his state. Carlson calls him one of the last independent journalists in Maine. Their film on the case is called High Crimes.

Robinson says Chinese cartels took over drug trade in the rural Northeast. He blames ignored border laws and failed local duty. The title also charges that politicians cover the trade up. Carlson presents the story as proof of a wider takeover. Listeners get a local reporter's case that stunned even a veteran host. The film extends the same case on screen.
podcast-tuckercarlson-LhqSdfw-enc:
Country star John Rich and comedian Russell Brand join Tucker Carlson together, and the announced theme is Christianity as the new counterculture: faith as rebellion in a secular age. The second thread is an accusation, that the neoconservatives are lying America into a third world war.

Rich brings the Nashville plain-spokenness his fans expect, Brand the theatrical sermonizing of his recent years, and Carlson the host's frame that joins them. All three men have remade themselves as faith-forward populists, and the episode functions as a summit of that tendency. War skepticism and revival preaching blend into one message: the old order lies, the old faith saves. Listeners get the movement's mood at full volume, from three of its most recognizable voices, arguing in friendly unison.
the-battle-of-principles-a-study-of-the-: Newell Dwight Hillis is named in a publisher's list of his works, where this title is described as a study of the heroism and eloquence of the anti-slavery conflict. the-complete-works-of-artemus-ward-part-: Stories and romances fill part 3 of Artemus Ward's complete works, at least by the record title's promise. Charles Farrar Browne is the man behind the Ward name. A Project Gutenberg header is all that stands here, complete with its standard legal warnings. No story or romance text follows it, so the part's contents rest on the title alone.
the-land-of-darkness-along-with-some-fur: Mrs. Oliphant published her vision of the afterlife with Macmillan in London in 1888, as a sequel to her Little Pilgrim stories. Only the title page and the first line of the contents are present here, naming the title piece that opens the volume. The chapters following the Little Pilgrim through darkness, and any later pieces in the book, do not appear in this record.
the-papers-and-writings-of-abraham-linco:
Volume Three of The Papers and Writings of Abraham Lincoln, in the Constitutional Edition edited by Arthur Brooks Lapsley, is given to the Lincoln-Douglas debates. It opens with Lincoln's speech at Springfield on June 17, 1858, at the close of the Republican State Convention that named him for the United States Senate. Douglas was not present.

Lincoln argues that slavery agitation will not cease until a crisis is reached and passed. A house divided against itself cannot stand, he says. The government cannot endure permanently half slave and half free. It will become all one thing or all the other. He then traces the Nebraska doctrine and the Dred Scott decision as parts of one legal machine.

Volume Four of The Papers and Writings of Abraham Lincoln, in the Constitutional Edition edited by Arthur Brooks Lapsley, continues the Lincoln-Douglas debates. The pages present open with the fourth debate, at Charleston on September 18, 1858. Lincoln begins by asking the huge crowd for silence so his words can be heard.

He then answers a question put to him at his hotel that day. In the speech as printed, Lincoln states that he is not in favor of social and political equality between the white and black races, nor of negro voters, jurors, or office holders. He adds that a man need not want a negro woman for a slave to refuse her for a wife. The volume preserves his 1858 words as spoken.
the-religion-of-numa-and-other-essays-on:
Jesse Benedict Carter gathers five essays on Roman religion. Macmillan issued the volume in 1906. The essays move from the religion of Numa onward. They cover the reorganization of Servius. They cover the coming of the Sibyl. A decline of faith and an Augustan renaissance close the set. The first essay argues a general rule. Rome grew by contact with the outside world.

Carter compares two ages of such contact. The republic met Greece through the Punic wars. The kings met foreign influence still earlier. That earlier wave changed the later kingdom deeply. Change through contact is his key to early Roman faith. Readers gain a clear frame for the essays. It suits anyone asking how religions absorb outside ideas.
tom-swift-and-his-great-searchlight-or-o: On the Border for Uncle Sam puts the Tom Swift great searchlight story by Victor Appleton on patrol, presented through twenty-five chapter headings. A scrap of paper, a spy in town, and searching for smugglers lead to an appeal for Tom's help. Later headings bring a raid, Andy's new airship, a rescue on a lake, a missing Ned, and a night race ending in capture. Chapter one, A Scrap of Paper, is announced without any text following. The contents list alone is included in this record.
your-child-today-and-tomorrow-some-probl: Sidonie Matzner Gruenberg wrote this guide for parents, in a second revised edition covering 1912 to 1920 printings. Pages present here hold title pages, her dedication to her mother and children, and the first line of a foreword by Bishop John H. Vincent. The title page lists the problems treated, from punishment, lies, and fear to work, play, imagination, and adolescence. The chapters themselves do not appear in these pages.
